reviewNote: tedious vs tiresome are close; tiresome stresses worn-out patience.

words.definition: Not interesting or exciting.
words.example: The lecture was rather dull.
words.whyHere: The mildest: simply lacking interest or spark.

words.definition: Making you feel tired and uninterested.
words.example: It was a boring afternoon.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'dull': it actively bores you.

words.definition: Boring and lasting a long time.
words.example: Filling forms is a tedious task.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'boring': dull and tiringly long.

words.definition: So boring it wears out your patience.
words.example: His constant complaints grew tiresome.
words.whyHere: The peak: dull enough to truly annoy.

reviewNote: beg vs implore are close; implore adds earnest, heartfelt pleading.

words.definition: To say you want an answer or help.
words.example: May I ask a quick question?
words.whyHere: The mildest: a simple, neutral request.

words.definition: To ask for something politely or formally.
words.example: They request a reply by Friday.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'ask': formal and deliberate.

words.definition: To ask for something in an anxious, urgent way.
words.example: The child began to beg for help.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'request': anxious and pleading.

words.definition: To beg someone very earnestly.
words.example: They implore the king to show mercy.
words.whyHere: The peak: a desperate, heartfelt plea.

reviewNote: chuckle vs giggle is soft; ordered by openness, then rising volume.

words.definition: To laugh quietly to yourself.
words.example: He read the note and began to chuckle.
words.whyHere: The mildest: a soft, private laugh.

words.definition: To laugh in a light, silly way.
words.example: The children started to giggle together.
words.whyHere: More open than a 'chuckle', light and playful.

words.definition: To make sounds that show you find something funny.
words.example: We laugh at his jokes.
words.whyHere: The plain, full sound of finding something funny.

words.definition: To laugh very loudly.
words.example: The crowd began to guffaw at the clown.
words.whyHere: The peak: a loud, hearty burst of laughter.

words.definition: Pleasant and friendly.
words.example: She is always nice to newcomers.
words.whyHere: The mildest: generally pleasant and friendly.

words.definition: Caring and gentle toward others.
words.example: It was kind of you to help.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'nice': real care for others.

words.definition: Showing that you worry about others' needs.
words.example: He is a caring older brother.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'kind': active concern for others.

words.definition: Feeling deep care for those who suffer.
words.example: The compassionate nurse comforted every patient.
words.whyHere: The peak: deep kindness toward others' pain.

reviewNote: welcoming vs hospitable are close; hospitable stresses care for guests.

words.definition: Nice and agreeable.
words.example: She gave a pleasant smile.
words.whyHere: The mildest: agreeable but not especially warm.

words.definition: Kind and behaving like a friend.
words.example: Our new neighbour is very friendly.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'pleasant': openly kind.

words.definition: Making others feel accepted and at ease.
words.example: The staff were warm and welcoming.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'friendly': actively puts others at ease.

words.definition: Generous and friendly to guests.
words.example: Our hosts were wonderfully hospitable.
words.whyHere: The peak: goes out of the way for guests.

reviewNote: slash vs hack are close; hack adds rough, repeated heavy blows.

words.definition: To cut something with small, quick strokes.
words.example: She began to snip the loose threads.
words.whyHere: The mildest: small, neat little cuts.

words.definition: To divide or open with a sharp edge.
words.example: Please cut the bread into slices.
words.whyHere: The plain, neutral word for using a blade.

words.definition: To cut with a long, violent stroke.
words.example: He tried to slash the thick rope.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'cut': a fast, forceful stroke.

words.definition: To cut roughly with heavy blows.
words.example: They had to hack through the branches.
words.whyHere: The peak: rough, heavy, repeated cutting.

reviewNote: devastate vs annihilate are close; annihilate implies a total wipeout.

words.definition: To harm something so it works less well.
words.example: Water can damage old books.
words.whyHere: The mildest: it causes harm but not ruin.

words.definition: To damage something so badly it is unusable.
words.example: The crash could wreck the car.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'damage': it ruins the thing.

words.definition: To damage something so completely it no longer exists.
words.example: Fire can destroy a whole forest.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'wreck': it is completely gone.

words.definition: To destroy or ruin something on a wide scale.
words.example: A flood can devastate an entire town.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'destroy': ruin across a wide area.

words.definition: To destroy something totally, leaving nothing.
words.example: The blast could annihilate the whole building.
words.whyHere: The peak: wiped out utterly, nothing left.

reviewNote: swift vs rapid are close; ordered by force and scale of motion.

words.definition: Done in a short time.
words.example: She gave a quick reply.
words.whyHere: The mildest: simply not slow.

words.definition: Moving or acting at high speed.
words.example: He drives a fast car.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'quick': clearly high speed.

words.definition: Moving very fast and smoothly.
words.example: The swift river carried the boat.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'fast': fast and graceful.

words.definition: Happening very quickly.
words.example: The town saw rapid growth.
words.whyHere: The peak: extremely quick change or motion.

reviewNote: inferno vs conflagration are close; conflagration stresses vast spread.

words.definition: A tiny bit of burning material.
words.example: A single spark started the fire.
words.whyHere: The smallest: a tiny fleck of fire.

words.definition: A bright tongue of burning gas.
words.example: A small flame rose from the match.
words.whyHere: Bigger than a 'spark': a visible burning flame.

words.definition: A large controlled outdoor fire.
words.example: We built a bonfire on the beach.
words.whyHere: Larger than a 'flame': a full, sizeable fire.

words.definition: A huge, dangerous fire.
words.example: The building became a raging inferno.
words.whyHere: Stronger than a 'bonfire': a large, dangerous blaze.

words.definition: An extremely large and destructive fire.
words.example: The conflagration destroyed the whole district.
words.whyHere: The peak: a vast, devastating fire.

reviewNote: crisis vs catastrophe are close; catastrophe adds severe, lasting damage.

words.definition: A small problem or difficulty.
words.example: We hit a small snag with the plan.
words.whyHere: The mildest: a minor, easily fixed problem.

words.definition: Something that causes trouble and needs solving.
words.example: The engine has a serious problem.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'snag': it truly needs solving.

words.definition: A time of great danger or difficulty.
words.example: The company faced a money crisis.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'problem': urgent and dangerous.

words.definition: A terrible event causing great damage.
words.example: The flood was a catastrophe for the region.
words.whyHere: The peak: a disaster with severe harm.

reviewNote: crucial vs vital are close; vital stresses being absolutely necessary.

words.definition: Of very little importance.
words.example: We argued over a trivial detail.
words.whyHere: The lowest: barely matters at all.

words.definition: Small and not very important.
words.example: It was only a minor change.
words.whyHere: A bit more than 'trivial', but still small.

words.definition: Mattering a lot; having a big effect.
words.example: This is an important decision.
words.whyHere: Clearly matters and deserves attention.

words.definition: Extremely important for success.
words.example: Water is crucial for life.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'important': success depends on it.

words.definition: Absolutely necessary.
words.example: Sleep is vital for good health.
words.whyHere: The peak: essential, cannot be done without.

reviewNote: weird vs bizarre are close; bizarre adds a surprising, extreme oddness.

words.definition: A little strange or unusual.
words.example: That is an odd thing to say.
words.whyHere: The mildest: slightly out of the ordinary.

words.definition: Unusual and hard to explain.
words.example: We heard a strange noise upstairs.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'odd': clearly unusual.

words.definition: Very strange and unsettling.
words.example: The house had a weird atmosphere.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'strange': oddly unsettling.

words.definition: Extremely strange and surprising.
words.example: He told a bizarre story.
words.whyHere: The peak: so strange it astonishes.

words.definition: A small area of still water.
words.example: Ducks swam on the village pond.
words.whyHere: The smallest: a little pool of water.

words.definition: A large area of water surrounded by land.
words.example: They sailed across the calm lake.
words.whyHere: Bigger than a 'pond': a broad inland water.

words.definition: A very large area of salt water.
words.example: We swam in the warm sea.
words.whyHere: Bigger than a 'lake': a vast salt water.

words.definition: The largest area of salt water on Earth.
words.example: Ships crossed the wide ocean.
words.whyHere: The peak: the biggest body of water.

reviewNote: glimmer vs glow are close; glow is steadier and warmer.

words.definition: To shine with a faint, unsteady light.
words.example: A candle can glimmer in the dark.
words.whyHere: The mildest: a weak, flickering light.

words.definition: To give out a soft, steady light.
words.example: The embers still glow at night.
words.whyHere: Steadier than a 'glimmer': a gentle, warm light.

words.definition: To give out or reflect bright light.
words.example: The stars shine over the hills.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'glow': clear, bright light.

words.definition: To shine or burn very brightly.
words.example: The lights blaze across the stadium.
words.whyHere: The peak: fierce, dazzling light.

reviewNote: grotesque vs monstrous are close; monstrous adds a frightening quality.

words.definition: Not attractive; ordinary in appearance.
words.example: It was a plain grey building.
words.whyHere: The mildest: simply not attractive.

words.definition: Unpleasant to look at.
words.example: They tore down the ugly old shed.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'plain': clearly unpleasant to see.

words.definition: Extremely ugly and shocking.
words.example: The old mask looked hideous.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'ugly': ugliness that shocks.

words.definition: So ugly it looks strange and disturbing.
words.example: The statue had a grotesque face.
words.whyHere: Stronger than 'hideous': ugly, weird, and disturbing.

words.definition: Frighteningly ugly, like a monster.
words.example: A monstrous shape loomed in the fog.
words.whyHere: The peak: ugliness that is truly frightening.
